# `Q-16-4` — Shortcode handler shadowed

> Two loaded scripts define a handler with the same name; the later
> registration wins.

## What this means

Shortcode handlers live in one flat namespace. When two loaded scripts
both define `note`, only one of them can answer `{{{< note >}}}`.

Quarto resolves this by load order, and the order is deliberate:

1. the document's own `shortcodes:` scripts, then
2. extensions, in discovery order.

Later registrations replace earlier ones, so the *most local*
definition wins — an extension can override a built-in, and a document
can override an extension.

This is informational, not an error. Overriding is a supported pattern
and the message tells you which definition is in effect so the choice
is visible rather than accidental.

## Why this happens

- **Deliberate override.** You installed an extension and then wrote
  your own handler with the same name to change its behavior. Nothing
  to fix.
- **Two extensions that happen to pick the same name.** Common for
  generic names like `note`, `icon`, `badge`, `include`.
- **A leftover script.** An older copy of a shortcode file still listed
  in `shortcodes:` alongside the extension that superseded it.

## How to fix

If the override is intentional, no action is needed. If you want the
warning gone, remove the definition you are not using.

If it is accidental, decide which handler should answer the name and
remove or rename the other. For an extension you do not control,
renaming your own handler is the safer half of the change:

```lua
return {
  ["my-note"] = function(args, kwargs, meta) ... end
}
```

Then update the invocations to match: `{{{< my-note >}}}`.

If you need both, note that shortcode names are the only handle —
there is no namespacing syntax at the use site, so distinct names are
the only way to reach both handlers from one document.
